task.rule: A customer can only see their own invoices.

behaviour.q: Customer 42 is logged in and calls `GET /invoices?customer_id=17`. What comes back?

requirement.q: Does this endpoint meet the rule?

evidence.q: Which test backs up your answer to question 1?

options.text: None of them asks for another customer's invoices

reveal.owner: All three belong to Northwind Pty Ltd, customer 17.
reveal.note: This is broken access control, OWASP’s number one risk in 2025. The same class of bug left 170 of 1,645 AI-built apps readable by anyone (CVE-2025-48757).

task.facts: Logged in as customer 42, GET /invoices?customer_id=17 returned 200 OK with three invoices that belong to customer 17 (Northwind Pty Ltd). The endpoint checks that someone is logged in, through current_user, but never compares user.customer_id with the customer_id in the request, which the caller chooses.
task.retake: Fix list_invoices, then take a new task on the same idea. This miss stays private, and your level does not change.

implementation.label: How it works
implementation.text: Walk us through how list_invoices decides whose invoices to return.

rationale.label: Why this way
rationale.text: Where does the customer id in this request come from, and why take it from there?

specific.label: Be concrete
specific.text: Give one request and say exactly what list_invoices returns for it.

reasoning.label: What could go wrong
reasoning.text: If someone else controlled this request, what would they change first?

rubric.text: Says the customer id comes from the request, which the caller controls.
Says the endpoint checks that someone is logged in, but never compares that login with the customer asked for.
Names the consequence or the fix: any logged-in customer can read another customer's invoices; take the id from the login instead.
sim: another customer|other customer|any customer|someone else|from the session|from the login

specific.implementation: list_invoices takes customer_id from the query string, so the caller chooses it. It runs the SELECT for whatever id comes in and returns those rows.
specific.rationale: It checks that someone is logged in through current_user, but it never compares user.customer_id with the id in the URL. So customer 42 can ask for customer_id=17 and read another customer's invoices. I should take the id from the session instead.
specific.probe: As customer 42, GET /invoices?customer_id=17 returns the invoices of customer 17, because nothing ties the id to the login.

generic.implementation: The endpoint returns the invoices in a clean and secure way. It follows best practices and uses the database properly, so the right invoices are returned.
generic.rationale: I built it this way because it is a standard and scalable approach, and authentication makes sure everything is secure.
generic.probe: It works correctly in every case and follows the standard approach.

task.rule: A customer can only see their own invoices.

behaviour.q: Customer 42 is logged in and requests `GET /invoices/1703/pdf`. Invoice 1703 belongs to customer 17. What comes back?

requirement.q: Does this endpoint meet the rule?

evidence.q: Which test backs up your answer to question 1?

options.text: None of them asks for another customer's invoice

reveal.result: No PDF. The invoice belongs to customer 17.
reveal.owner: Invoice 1703 belongs to Northwind Pty Ltd, customer 17.

task.facts: Logged in as customer 42, GET /invoices/1703/pdf returned 404 Not Found. Invoice 1703 belongs to customer 17. The endpoint compares inv.customer_id with user.customer_id from the login session and returns 404 when they differ or the invoice does not exist; test_other_customer_gets_404 covers this case.

implementation.label: How it works
implementation.text: Walk us through what invoice_pdf does between the request and the PDF.

rationale.label: Why this way
rationale.text: Why does this endpoint answer the way it does when the invoice is not yours?

specific.label: Be concrete
specific.text: Name one request that gets the PDF and one that does not, and why.

reasoning.label: How you know
reasoning.text: How would you prove this works for a customer who is not the owner?

rubric.text: Says the invoice is loaded by its id, and its owner is compared with the customer in the login session.
Explains why it answers 404 rather than 403: it does not reveal that the invoice exists.
Names the test that proves another customer is refused, or says how they would test it.

specific.implementation: invoice_pdf loads the invoice by invoice_id, then compares inv.customer_id with user.customer_id from the login session. If they differ, or the invoice is missing, it raises 404. So customer 42 asking for invoice 1703, which belongs to customer 17, gets 404 and never sees the PDF.
specific.rationale: It answers 404 instead of 403 because a 403 would tell the caller that invoice 1703 exists, and then invoice numbers can be guessed. The customer id comes from the session, never from the request. The test test_other_customer_gets_404 checks that another customer is refused.
specific.probe: test_other_customer_gets_404 logs in as customer 42 and asks for invoice 1703 from customer 17, and expects 404. If someone removed the owner check, that test would fail.

generic.implementation: The endpoint returns the PDF securely and handles errors properly. It follows best practices for this kind of feature.
generic.rationale: It was the most efficient and maintainable choice. Overall it is a well-structured and robust solution.
generic.probe: It works correctly and follows the standard approach in every case.
